newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Fighting resumes as Zaire rebels tighten grip.
newsitem.headline: Fighting resumes as Zaire rebels tighten grip.

text.p: Heavy automatic gunfire rattled around the lush hills to the west of this deserted camp on Saturday as rebels pursued Hutu fighters deeper into Zaire.
In the distance, sporadic mortar and artillery explosions could be heard.
The Hutus -- ex-Rwandan army soldiers and members of the dreaded Interahamwe militia -- fled into the bush to escape a relentless bombardment by Zairean rebels earlier this week.

Spent cartridge cases littering the ground and unused mortars scattered on the floor of nearby buildings were the only signs that remained of their presence in this training camp from where they plotted a return to power.

Chief culprits for the slaughter of up to one million people, mostly Tutsis, in Rwanda's 1994 genocide, the fighters convinced or forced hundreds of thousands of fellow Hutus to remain with them as human shields.
Their hold on the refugees in nearby Mugunga camp, now flooding back into Rwanda, was broken by a lightning strike through eastern Zaire by rebels, who have close links with Rwanda, four weeks ago.
The last straw was a fierce rocket, mortar and heavy artillery bombardment on Thursday which set off a human tidal wave of ordinary refugees towards Rwanda on Friday.

On Saturday groups of Zairean rebel soldiers lounged around the entrance to the burned and pillaged Mugunga camp. Others patrolled the road from the north leading to Mugunga, once-teeming with 400,000 refugees.
In the middle of that camp, next to a collection of Oxfam water tanks, was a pile of some 27 bodies -- all women and children, apart from one man.
They had been hacked to death with machetes.
In the middle, the body of a boy -- around eight years old -- stirred slightly. He was breathing despite a deep machete wound in his skull from where his brains oozed out.
Some 100 metres (yds) away, lay three more bodies -- a man, woman and child.
It was not clear if they had been killed by rebels forcing the Rwandans to go home or by Hutu gunmen in a last, desperate bid to make them stay.
Outside Mugunga camp, the roads were blocked with tens of thousands of refugees heading home. Many appeared to be suffering from chronic hunger and thirst and begged passing vehicles for food.

Aid workers say since the exodus began on Friday some 200,000 people had returned to Rwanda and at least 10,000 an hour were still crossing the border. At midday Saturday the road from Zaire was still thick with people for several kilometres (miles).

Along the sides of the road, there were a few isolated cases of dehydration, exhaustion, fatigue and heat stroke. But among a flow of perhaps 250,000 people, a Reuters correspondent counted only six clearly sick people.

Aid workers in Rwanda said the returnees were generally in good physical and mental shape. At Goma's central hospital doctor Augustin Karumba said one cholera case had been confirmed while others were waiting for the results of laboratory tests.
